lesson.title: The Wall Outside the Membrane: Why So Many Cells Build Their Own Armor
lesson.summary: The cell wall is a rigid layer outside the plasma membrane, built from different materials in bacteria, archaea, fungi, and plants, that provides shape and protects the cell from bursting under osmotic pressure.
lesson.body:
Prokaryotic cells generally lack the internal membrane-bound organelles of eukaryotes, but most of them compensate with something eukaryotic animal cells never evolved: a rigid cell wall wrapped around the outside of the plasma membrane. The wall is not optional decoration. Prokaryotic cells routinely live in environments where the surrounding fluid is more dilute than their cytoplasm, so water tends to rush in by osmosis. Without something to resist that inward pressure, the plasma membrane would stretch and the cell would lyse. The cell wall acts like a pressure vessel, holding a firm shape against that osmotic push.

In most bacteria, the wall is built from peptidoglycan, a mesh made of long sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides, forming a single giant, bag-shaped molecule that encases the entire cell. The thickness of that peptidoglycan layer is the basis of the Gram stain: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that traps crystal violet dye, while Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner peptidoglycan layer sandwiched between the plasma membrane and an additional outer membrane, so they lose the purple stain and pick up a pink counterstain instead. This is also why the antibiotic penicillin works: it blocks an enzyme needed to cross-link peptidoglycan, so growing bacterial cells cannot build a wall strong enough to contain their internal pressure and they burst.

Archaea, though prokaryotic, generally do not use peptidoglycan at all. Many build walls from a different material called pseudopeptidoglycan or from other polymers such as glycoproteins, a molecular difference that was one of the early clues that archaea are a distinct domain of life from bacteria rather than just another bacterial lineage.

Cell walls are not exclusive to prokaryotes. Fungal cells build walls out of chitin, the same tough polysaccharide found in insect exoskeletons, while plant cells build walls primarily from cellulose, long chains of glucose bundled into strong fibers. A plant cell wall is typically layered: a flexible primary wall laid down while the cell is still growing, and in some cells a rigid secondary wall added later, often reinforced with lignin, once growth has stopped. Because the shared function across all of these very different materials is the same, resisting osmotic pressure and giving the cell a defined shape, the cell wall is a striking case of convergent solutions to the same physical problem.

The wall also explains familiar, everyday phenomena. A wilted houseplant that perks back up after watering is showing what happens when its cells regain enough internal water pressure, called turgor pressure, to push against a wall that has not gone anywhere. Because a rigid wall sits directly outside the plasma membrane, it also constrains how neighboring plant cells can communicate directly, which is exactly the problem solved by the channels discussed next.
